title: Hermits and consecrated virgins

segments.voice: Yesterday, deacons: diakonos, a servant, and the seven chosen to feed the widows. Your line was servants. Whose glass did you fill without mentioning it? Day one thousand four hundred eleven.

A hospital pharmacist finishes her shift, takes the bus home to a small apartment, and prays the evening prayer of the Church at her kitchen table. On her right hand is a plain ring. Years ago, in her cathedral, the bishop consecrated her to Christ, and she went back to work the next morning. A few hours' drive away, a man lives alone in a cabin on land his diocese lent him. He has made vows into the hands of his bishop. He grows vegetables, keeps silence, and prays through the night for a world that mostly doesn't know he's there. Neither one belongs to an order. Both callings reach back to the early Church. Today, hermits and consecrated virgins.
screen: `A PHARMACIST WITH A PLAIN RING.` → `A CABIN, A VOW, A SILENCE.` → `NEITHER BELONGS TO AN ORDER.`

segments.voice: Start with the hermit. The prophet Elijah, worn out and running for his life, goes a day's journey into the desert and then on to the mountain of God, and the Lord isn't in the wind, or the earthquake, or the fire. In the Douay-Rheims: "and after the fire a whistling of a gentle air." Hermits go looking for that whisper. In the early centuries, tradition says, men and women went out into the Egyptian desert to pray alone; the Life of Antony tells of one of them. The Catechism describes hermits today: they give their lives to the praise of God and the salvation of the world through a stricter separation from the world, the silence of solitude, and constant prayer and penance. Church law recognizes a hermit who professes the evangelical counsels publicly in the hands of the diocesan bishop and lives under his guidance. Now the consecrated virgin. The Catechism says that from apostolic times, Christian virgins, called by the Lord, gave themselves to him with an undivided heart. The Church keeps a rite for it today. A woman who has never married is consecrated by her bishop in a solemn liturgy, and she is joined to Christ as a bride. She may live in a community, or she may live in the world, at her own job, in her own apartment, under the bishop's care. So two old callings sit in plain sight. One hidden in a cabin. One hidden on a bus. The Catechism calls the hermit's life a reminder of the inward side of the Church's mystery: what is quietly happening with God underneath.
screen: `ELIJAH IN THE DESERT.` · `A WHISTLING OF A GENTLE AIR.` · `VOWS INTO THE BISHOP'S HANDS.` · `A VIRGIN CONSECRATED IN THE WORLD.` · then, large: `AFTER THE FIRE, A WHISTLING OF A GENTLE AIR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for hidden vocations. Settle, and breathe. Somewhere today a hermit is keeping silence, and a woman with a plain ring is at work, and nobody around them knows. Let the quiet of this sit be a small share in theirs. Leave your phone face down. Listen to the room, and then under the room. If you pray, you can ask God to strengthen people whose callings no one sees, and to keep them faithful. If you don't, simply hold them in mind, unnamed, with good will. The bell holds the time.

Hermits and consecrated virgins. Callings from the Church's early centuries, still lived today: solitude and prayer under a bishop, and lifelong consecration to Christ, sometimes in the middle of ordinary life. Today's word.
Your line: ancient callings. Today, find five minutes of real silence, no screen, no sound, and spend them the way a hermit might: listening for the gentle air. Day one thousand four hundred eleven.

howItsDone: Diocesan hermits profess the evangelical counsels publicly before their bishop and live in solitude, silence and prayer under his guidance. Consecrated virgins are consecrated by their bishop in a solemn rite and may live in community or in the world, some keeping their ordinary jobs.

fork.setup: you're a woman who has never married. you want to give your whole life to Christ, but you don't feel called to a religious order, and you love your job. what does the Church offer?
options: nothing: give your life to Christ means joining an order.
consecration by your bishop as a consecrated virgin, living in the world.
a private promise that the Church never recognizes.
fork.reveal: an ancient calling the Church still keeps: the bishop consecrates her, and she can keep her job and home under his care.

original.note: Greek, desert or wilderness: where Elijah fled, and where tradition says the early hermits went to pray.

trapdoor: what you thought: hermits and consecrated virgins are figures from old paintings.
what it means: two early callings still lived now: solitude under a bishop, and consecration to Christ in the middle of the world.

what a scholar hears: the Catechism on hermits (CCC 920–921) and on consecrated virgins 'from apostolic times' (CCC 922–924); Canon 603 on diocesan hermits; the rite of consecration to a life of virginity.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of 3 Kings (1 Kings) 19:12: confirm 'and after the fire a whistling of a gentle air.'
'Hermit' from Greek erēmos (desert), via erēmitēs: standard dictionary derivation; confirm.
Desert hermits in Egypt given as 'tradition says' with the Life of Antony named, not quoted; confirm.

CCC 920–921 (hermits; stricter separation from the world, silence of solitude, assiduous prayer and penance; a reminder of the interior aspect of the Church's mystery) and CCC 922–924 (virgins 'from apostolic times'; consecrated by the diocesan bishop; mystically espoused to Christ) paraphrased; confirm.
Canon 603 (diocesan hermits profess the counsels in the hands of the bishop) and canon 604 (order of virgins): confirm.
'The practice faded, and after the Second Vatican Council the Church restored a rite for it': confirm wording (the rite for women living in the world was restored after the Council).
Hook: the ring given in the rite, and the two people described, are illustrative; confirm that a ring is among the insignia of consecration.
